issues.subcategory: impossible generation slope summary
issues.description: The reported generation effect on wheel speed is internally inconsistent with the reported first- and fifth-generation means. A mean generation effect of 5.37 m/h cannot plausibly produce an increase from 123.6 to 145.7 m/h across four generation steps (difference ≈22.1 m/h, or ≈5.5 m/h/generation if linear), yet the accompanying 95% interval of (1.58, 9.02) appears to refer to a slope while the text labels it as an average wheel speed. The phrasing makes the estimand ambiguous and numerically inconsistent with the descriptive results.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations (Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h, Figure 2.A) ... The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h ... After 5 generations, average wheel speed increased to 145.7 m/h

issues.subcategory: credible interval mislabeled as confidence interval
issues.description: The manuscript states that Bayesian multilevel models were used and that 95% credible intervals were used for inference, but the results repeatedly report '95% Confidence Intervals'. In a Bayesian analysis, these should be credible intervals unless a separate frequentist analysis was run. This mislabeling obscures the inferential framework and could mislead readers about the meaning of the intervals.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.subcategory: mixed use of CI and HPDI without clarification
issues.description: The paper alternates between '95% Confidence Intervals' for model coefficients and '95% Highest Posterior Density Interval' for generation means, without explaining why different interval types are used within the same Bayesian framework. This is confusing and suggests either inconsistent reporting or unreported post hoc estimation procedures.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed ... increased across generations (Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02) ... The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h (95% Highest Posterior Density Interval: (117.3, 130.6))

issues.subcategory: linear model for bounded count outcome
issues.description: Understanding score is a discrete bounded variable based on 10 pairwise judgments, yet it is modeled with a linear model. This ignores the bounded/count nature of the data and may yield inappropriate distributional assumptions, heteroskedasticity, and uninterpretable linear effects. A binomial or ordinal model would be more appropriate, especially given chance-level benchmarks are discussed.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Score” as the outcome variable, “Generation” as a predictor variable and “Chain’s identity” as a random effect

issues.subcategory: linear model for zero-inflated speed data
issues.description: Wheel speed includes structural zeros for failures in Analysis 3 ('Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0'), yet a linear Gaussian model was fitted. This mixture of positive continuous values and excess zeros violates standard linear-model assumptions; a hurdle, two-part, or censored model would better represent the process.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials ... We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable

issues.subcategory: inconsistent handling of failure trials across analyses
issues.description: Failure trials are handled differently across analyses in a way that affects comparability. In Analysis 1, data were restricted to last two trials 'to limit the occurrence' of non-descending wheels, but failures are not clearly included or excluded; in Analysis 3, failures are explicitly coded as speed 0. This inconsistency means treatment and within-treatment analyses are not directly comparable and may bias conclusions about generational change and treatment effects.
issues.quote: Analysis 1 ... Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset... Analysis 3 ... Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend

issues.subcategory: post hoc model selection after comparing candidate models
issues.description: The final model for preregistered Analysis 1 was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to observed data. This introduces researcher degrees of freedom not fully specified in the preregistration and undermines the confirmatory status of the analysis, especially because model-comparison criteria and candidate set are not described here.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.subcategory: nonconverged preregistered model replaced with aggregated score analysis
issues.description: A preregistered analysis was abandoned because the model did not converge, and the authors instead aggregated across physical principles and removed preregistered terms. Aggregating a theoretically important distinction (inertia vs centre of mass) can materially change conclusions and masks the very dissociation later emphasized in exploratory analyses. The replacement analysis is effectively post hoc and should be clearly framed as such and justified with sensitivity analyses.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: confirmatory claim stronger than reported evidence
issues.description: The abstract and discussion make strong claims that theory transmission has 'no noticeable effect' and 'did not help', yet the reported interaction for understanding excludes zero and is described as participants in the very last generation having 'slightly better understanding'. The manuscript downplays this nonzero estimate while using broad null-sounding language elsewhere.
issues.quote: Moreover, we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution.

issues.subcategory: generalization to mixed-gender settings unsupported and contradicted by design
issues.description: The discussion claims findings generalize beyond single-sex chains to mixed-gender collaborative settings, but the study only used sex-segregated chains and did not test mixed-gender groups. This is an unsupported extrapolation and also contradicts the methods description.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.subcategory: unsupported extrapolation from WEIRD student sample to human technology broadly
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames conclusions in terms of human technological evolution and archaeological interpretation, but the sample is limited to French university students optimizing a highly simplified laboratory wheel task over five trials. Such a task may model some aspects of cumulative optimization, but broad claims about 'complex technologies' and human cultural evolution require stronger justification and acknowledgement of the narrow population and task context.
issues.quote: These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.subcategory: understanding measure may not capture causal understanding
issues.description: The main claim hinges on 'causal understanding', yet the test operationalizes this as choosing which wheel of a pair will be faster. This can be solved by pattern recognition, remembered heuristics, or task-specific cue use without an explicit causal model, and conversely may fail to capture deeper understanding of tradeoffs or mechanism. The measure therefore has limited construct validity for the broad construct 'explicit causal understanding'.
issues.quote: Participants’ understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to estimate how long each wheel would take to reach the bottom of the rails.

issues.subcategory: chance level and scoring scheme insufficiently specified
issues.description: Participants could answer 'Wheel 1', 'Wheel 2' or 'No difference', but the scoring scheme for the understanding test is not reported. Because there are three response options, the expected score under random guessing depends on whether 'No difference' is ever correct and on the composition of item types. Without explicit scoring rules and item answer keys, the interpretation of scores and the chance benchmark is unclear.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: “Wheel 1”, “Wheel 2” or “No difference”.

issues.subcategory: missing details of understanding score computation
issues.description: The manuscript never explains exactly how the 10 understanding items were scored, whether 'No difference' was ever correct, whether partial credit was used, or how aggregated and subscale scores were computed. This omission prevents replication and evaluation of the validity of the understanding analyses.
issues.quote: The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

issues.subcategory: causal claim about theory constraining exploration from nonrandom inherited-theory categories
issues.description: The exploratory comparison of participants who inherited inertia vs centre-of-mass theories is observational within the theory-treatment arm. Inherited theory content depends on what prior participants happened to write, which may correlate with chain history, wheel configurations inherited, generation, and other unmeasured factors. Therefore, claims that inheriting a given theory 'affected' exploration and understanding are not warranted without random assignment of theory content or stronger controls.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants’ exploration behavior ... Participants who inherited an inertia theory mainly produced compact and balanced wheels ... In contrast, participants who inherited a centre-of-mass theory produced unbalanced wheels

issues.subcategory: mediation/mechanism claim unsupported
issues.description: The authors infer that theory transmission canalizes exploration, which then shapes understanding, but no formal mediation analysis or randomized manipulation of exploration is presented. The supplementary grouping analysis among Configurations participants is descriptive and does not establish that exploration caused the understanding differences or that inherited theory caused exploration differences independently of other chain-level factors.
issues.quote: These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration.

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding in data collection and analysis
issues.description: The experimenter both implemented wheel configurations physically and was not blind to condition; analyses were also not blind. This opens the possibility of expectancy effects, subtle procedural differences, or analytic bias. Such risks are particularly relevant when one condition includes written theories and when the experimenter manually positions apparatus components.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments... Data analyses were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: sample-size justification inadequate and no power analysis
issues.description: The study explicitly states no statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size and justifies N by comparison to prior publications. This does not establish adequate power for the preregistered treatment-by-generation interaction or for exploratory subgroup analyses, several of which involve very small cells (e.g., full theory N=6).
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications30,31.

issues.subcategory: underpowered exploratory subgroups
issues.description: Several exploratory conclusions rest on extremely small subgroups, especially the 'full theory' category (N=6). Such cell sizes are unstable and highly sensitive to outliers and chain-specific idiosyncrasies, making graphical patterns unreliable for inference.
issues.quote: Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory ... 6 inherited a full theory

issues.subcategory: missing randomization details
issues.description: The manuscript says participants were randomly assigned to condition and chain, and the organization of experimental conditions was randomized, but does not explain the randomization procedure, allocation concealment, blocking, or whether assignment was balanced over time. These details matter because sessions were individual and sequential, creating possible time-related confounds.
issues.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one condition of the experiment and one sex-segregated chain... The organization of experimental conditions was randomized.

issues.subcategory: confounding by sex-segregated chain structure
issues.description: Chains were exclusively male or exclusively female, yet sex is neither modeled nor discussed as a possible source of variation. Because chain is the unit of cultural transmission and each chain is single-sex, any sex-related behavioral differences are perfectly confounded with chain composition, limiting interpretability and generalizability.
issues.quote: In each treatment, participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females).

issues.subcategory: failure trials treated ad hoc rather than modeled as missing/not missing process
issues.description: Non-descending wheels represent an important outcome but are not modeled directly; instead they are partly reduced by restricting data to later trials and elsewhere coded as speed 0. This ad hoc handling conflates failure probability with speed and ignores a potentially informative missingness/structural-zero process relevant to optimization and social learning.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset... Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent track length/speed definitions
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between a 1-meter track, 92 cm between switches, and 'about one meter', yet reports speed as 1m/descent time. If timing is based on the 92 cm switch interval, using 1 m in the speed calculation would systematically mis-scale all speeds. The exact distance used for speed computation should be stated and consistent.
issues.quote: The physical system was a wheel that traveled down a 1-meter long inclined track... Two push-button switches ... were located 92 cm apart on the rails... The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time)

issues.subcategory: optimization percentage appears miscalculated/undefined
issues.description: The claim of '71% optimization after only four cultural generations' is unclear and apparently inconsistent with the reported numbers. Depending on baseline and ceiling used, the increase from 123.6 to 145.7 relative to a 154 m/h maximum is not 71%. The manuscript does not define the denominator for this percentage, making the statistic uninterpretable.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: maximum possible speed not established in main text
issues.description: The manuscript invokes a 'maximum possible speed' of about 154 m/h but does not explain how this value was determined, whether analytically or empirically, or its uncertainty. Since ceiling proximity is central to the interpretation of 'highly optimized', the basis for the optimum should be explicitly reported in the main text.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h

issues.subcategory: oversimplified dichotomy between causal reasoning and cumulative culture
issues.description: The framing sets up a contrast between enhanced causal reasoning and cumulative cultural improvement, but these are not mutually exclusive. Even the authors note participants used nonrandom, potentially theory-laden intuitions. Concluding that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning overstates what this experiment shows about the interplay between individual cognition and cumulative culture.
issues.quote: These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.subcategory: post-task understanding test may be contaminated by training/exposure differences
issues.description: Understanding was assessed only after five optimization trials, during which participants had differential exposure to configurations, scores, and inherited theories. Thus the test conflates pre-existing understanding, learning from interaction, and memory for experienced configurations. Without a baseline measure, conclusions about 'absence of causal understanding' are limited.
issues.quote: This allowed us to rigorously measure participants’ causal understanding of the system after they completed their 5 trials

issues.subcategory: reward structure may alter exploration differently across generations
issues.description: Participants' payoff depended on both their own performance and the next participant’s first two wheels, and later participants knew their last two trials would be transmitted. This creates strategic incentives that may vary by generation and treatment, potentially affecting exploration independently of understanding. The manuscript does not analyze or control for these incentive-induced behavioral differences.
issues.quote: Participants were informed that their last two trials would be transmitted to the next participant in the chain, and that their reward depended both on their own performance and on the performance of the next participant in the chain.

issues.subcategory: missing details of candidate models and priors
issues.description: For Bayesian multilevel analyses, priors, diagnostics, convergence statistics, posterior predictive checks, and exact candidate models are not reported in the manuscript text. Since model choice and convergence problems affected results, these omissions hamper critical evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33

issues.subcategory: theory-coding reliability incomplete
issues.description: Cohen's kappa is reported for two binary coding dimensions, but the manuscript does not describe how disagreements were resolved, whether coders were blind to treatment/generation/chain, or provide reliability for the four-category collapsed variable used in results. These details matter because theory categories underlie exploratory conclusions.
issues.quote: 3 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel ... Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.subcategory: causal language from correlational generation trends
issues.description: The paper frequently states that selective retention of improvements 'produces' optimized solutions and that cumulative culture emerges 'without the need' for understanding. Although the generational chain design is suggestive, there is no asocial control condition showing what optimization would occur without social transmission under identical repeated-trial opportunities, so attributing gains specifically to selective retention is incomplete.
issues.quote: This confirms that the retention of improvements over generations produces highly optimized solutions and need not depend on the emergence of more accurate causal models.

issues.subcategory: missing asocial/repeated-individual control
issues.description: The study lacks a control condition in which individuals or isolated participants receive the same number of optimization opportunities without social information. Without such a baseline, it is difficult to quantify the incremental contribution of cumulative cultural transmission versus individual trial-and-error learning or generic task practice.
issues.quote: All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain so as to simulate overlapping generations.

issues.subcategory: single task is low-dimensional and atypical of target domain
issues.description: The authors acknowledge the wheel problem is low-dimensional, yet they draw conclusions about many-dimensional technologies such as bows. A finding in a two-variable optimization task may not translate to high-dimensional cultural technologies where causal decomposition, modularity, and interaction effects differ substantially.
issues.quote: Finally, although the physics of the system are by no means trivial, the optimization problem is low-dimensional, which provides a conservative test of our hypotheses, compared to the many-dimensional problem of optimizing, for example, the performance of a bow

issues.subcategory: claim of ecological validity overstated
issues.description: The authors assert ecological validity because the system follows laws of physics rather than arbitrary rules, but ecological validity concerns resemblance to real-world contexts, not merely physical realism. A laboratory wheel with discrete slider-selected weights and only five trials is still far removed from most technological design contexts.
issues.quote: Second, the performance of the wheel depends solely on the laws of physics, and not on arbitrary principles that could compromise the ecological validity of our results.
